notes.front: What is a data centre, in one sentence?
notes.back: A building designed to house many computers, mostly servers, with backup power and cooling so they keep running through problems.
notes.explanation: Most applications people use every day run in data centres, and many data centres rent out their capacity to customers.
notes.example: Like a warehouse full of servers, with generators for power cuts and air conditioning to stop the machines overheating.

notes.front: What is cloud computing, in one sentence?
notes.back: Renting computing power, storage and network capacity on demand from data centres, instead of buying and running your own hardware.
notes.explanation: It removes the delay and cost of building new infrastructure, and lets an organisation add or remove resources as demand changes.
notes.example: Like hiring a car for the weekend instead of owning a fleet that sits idle most of the year.

notes.front: What is a CPU, in one sentence?
notes.back: A computer’s compute-processing resource, counted in cores, physical or virtual.
notes.explanation: CPU and memory are the most common compute resources that programs use; in Kubernetes, 1 CPU is 1 physical or 1 virtual core.
notes.example: A laptop with a four-core processor has four CPU cores to share among the programs it runs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Resource Management for Pods and Containers”, “Resource types” and “CPU resource units”

notes.front: What is an operating system, in one sentence?
notes.back: The software that runs the computer: it loads first when the machine starts, and programs rely on it for their basic work.
notes.explanation: Applications ask the operating system to handle things such as files and the screen, instead of controlling the hardware themselves.
notes.example: When a word processor saves your document, it asks the operating system to write the file to disk.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “operating system (OS)”, from NIST SP 800-44 Version 2

notes.front: What is a bare metal machine?
notes.back: A physical server running exactly one operating system directly on its hardware, with nothing in between.
notes.explanation: This is the original pattern of computing: all the machine’s resources go straight to one operating system, with no extra layer to slow it down.
notes.example: Like a house lived in by a single family: every room is theirs.

notes.front: What is a virtual machine (VM)?
notes.back: A computer made in software, with its own operating system, that runs on shared physical hardware alongside other VMs.
notes.explanation: Because a VM is not bound to its hardware, it can be created or destroyed in minutes and moved to another machine when one needs repair.
notes.example: Like flats in one building: each has its own front door and rooms, but they all share the same foundations.

notes.front: What is virtualisation (spelt “virtualization” in the sources)?
notes.back: Letting one physical computer run several isolated operating systems, each as a virtual machine with its own share of CPU, memory and network.
notes.explanation: Cloud computing is powered mainly by it: the “computer” you rent from a cloud provider is actually a VM.
notes.example: Like dividing one large office floor into separate lockable rooms for different tenants.

notes.front: What is a hypervisor?
notes.back: Software that divides a physical machine’s CPU, memory, network and storage into parts and allocates them to create virtual machines.
notes.explanation: It keeps each VM isolated, so a problem in one does not affect the others, and it hides the hardware’s low-level details.
notes.example: Like a building manager who splits one building into flats and makes sure each gets its own share of water and power.

notes.front: What is an API (application programming interface)?
notes.back: A defined way for computer programs to interact with each other.
notes.explanation: An API limits what can be asked of it, which keeps communication between programs stable and lets applications be built from parts that work together.
notes.example: As a web page lets a person use a website, an API lets one program use another.

notes.front: What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud service model that offers compute, storage and network resources on demand, paid for as you go.
notes.explanation: The cloud provider owns and runs the hardware, so you avoid buying and maintaining data centre space sized for peak demand.
notes.example: Renting virtual machines from a cloud provider by the hour and installing your own software on them.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)”

notes.front: What is Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud service where you deploy your own applications, built with the provider’s languages and tools, while the provider manages the infrastructure.
notes.explanation: You control your deployed applications, and perhaps some settings of the environment that hosts them, but not the network, servers, operating systems or storage.
notes.example: A developer uploads an app written in a language the provider supports, and the provider runs it; the developer never sets up a server.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Platform as a Service (PaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: What is Software as a Service (SaaS)?
notes.back: Using the provider’s applications, which run on its cloud infrastructure, from a web browser or through a program interface.
notes.explanation: You manage none of what lies beneath: not the network, servers, operating systems, storage or even the application’s features, apart perhaps from a few user settings.
notes.example: Web-based email: you use it in a browser, and the provider runs everything behind it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Software as a Service (SaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: What is a managed service?
notes.back: A software offering maintained by a third-party provider.
notes.explanation: It can be any software offering that an application can use, from computing capacity to a database or a messaging service.
notes.example: Azure SQL Database: a database an application can use, which Microsoft runs and maintains.

notes.front: What is a client-server architecture?
notes.back: An application split between a client that asks for work to be done and one or more servers that do it.
notes.explanation: Logic on the server can be updated without changing every client, and many clients can see and share the same data.
notes.example: Gmail in your web browser (the client) sends your email to Google’s computers (the servers), which deliver it.

notes.front: What is HTTP, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol: a standard method for communication between clients and web servers.
notes.explanation: It is the language of the web, and many APIs use it too, so programs can talk to servers the same way browsers do.
notes.example: Your browser sends an HTTP request for a page, and the web server sends the page back in an HTTP response.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)”, from NISTIR 7387

notes.front: What is REST, in one sentence?
notes.back: Representational State Transfer: a common style for designing the APIs of web services.
notes.explanation: An API built in this style is called RESTful; programs use it over HTTP, much as a browser fetches pages.
notes.example: A weather service with a RESTful API: other programs send it HTTP requests and get forecasts back.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Representational State Transfer (REST)”, from NIST SP 1800-16B

notes.front: In computing, what is a process?
notes.back: A program that is running (executing).
notes.explanation: The program is the file on disk; a process is that program at work, using CPU and memory.
notes.example: Opening a web browser starts a process; closing the browser ends it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “process”, from NIST SP 800-86

notes.front: What is a distributed system?
notes.back: Independent computers or processes, connected over a network, that together appear to users as one system.
notes.explanation: Some applications are too big for any single computer, and spreading the work means one failed machine need not stop everything.
notes.example: Gmail or Netflix: each looks like one service to you but runs on many connected computers.

notes.front: In computing generally, what is a node?
notes.back: One computer, physical or virtual, that works with other computers on a common task.
notes.explanation: A node is a distinct unit of CPU, memory and network that can be added to a group of computers.
notes.example: Your laptop, modem and printer on your home wifi are each a node.

notes.front: What is an IP address, in one sentence?
notes.back: The number that identifies where a machine is on a network, so data can be delivered to it.
notes.explanation: The Internet Protocol separates names from addresses: a name says what you want, an address says where it is.
notes.example: 10.0.0.11 is an IP address: four numbers separated by dots.
notes.sourceLicence: C · IETF Trust; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is DNS, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Domain Name System: the internet’s system for keeping track of domain names and the IP addresses behind them.
notes.explanation: People use names; DNS finds the IP address behind each name.
notes.example: Typing a website’s name into a browser works because DNS finds the IP address of the server behind it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Domain Name System (DNS)”, from NIST SP 1800-16B and RFC 1034

notes.front: In networking, what is a port?
notes.back: A number that identifies one application service on a machine, so traffic reaching its IP address finds the right program.
notes.explanation: One machine has one IP address but can run many network services at once; port numbers keep their traffic apart.
notes.example: A server runs a website and a database; each listens on its own port, and each request names the port it wants.
notes.source: IETF RFC 9293, “Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)”, §2.2 “Key TCP Concepts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · IETF Trust; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is a host, in network computing?
notes.back: A computer reachable over a network that “hosts” a service or application; for our purposes, much the same as a node.
notes.explanation: Hosts usually have a hostname and an IP address so other computers can find them.
notes.example: The server that runs a company’s website is that website’s host.

notes.front: In computing generally, what is a cluster?
notes.back: A group of nodes that work together towards a common goal.
notes.explanation: Software on a single computer has a single point of failure; running it across a cluster removes that weakness.
notes.example: Five computers sharing the work of one video website, so that it stays up if one of them crashes.

notes.front: In computing, what is an abstraction?
notes.back: A representation that hides the details of something, so that it is simpler to use.
notes.explanation: Systems stack several layers of abstraction; developers build against one layer without worrying about what lies underneath.
notes.example: Your laptop’s operating system: you run programs without knowing how the CPU and memory are handled.

notes.front: What is idempotence?
notes.back: The property of an operation that always leads to the same outcome, however many times you run it.
notes.explanation: Running an idempotent operation again with the same inputs has no additional effect.
notes.example: Pressing “off” on a light switch that is already off: the light stays off, just as after the first press.

notes.front: What is encryption, in one sentence?
notes.back: Turning readable data (plaintext) into a form (ciphertext) that hides its meaning from anyone but the intended recipient.
notes.explanation: Reversing it is called decryption; encryption protects data that others might see in transit or in storage.
notes.example: A card number sent encrypted over the internet looks like random characters to anyone who intercepts it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “encryption”, from NIST SP 800-82r3 (after RFC 4949) and NIST SP 800-101 Rev. 1

notes.front: What is TLS (Transport Layer Security)?
notes.back: A protocol that encrypts data sent over a network, so that third parties cannot read or alter it on the way.
notes.explanation: It also lets a client confirm the identity of the server it is calling, which reduces the risk of talking to a fraudulent site.
notes.example: The connection between your web browser and your bank’s website.

notes.front: What is a digital certificate?
notes.back: A digital document that shows an entity is who it says it is, and helps encrypt what is sent to it.
notes.explanation: On a network there is otherwise no guarantee that a device is who it claims to be.
notes.example: The padlock your web browser shows in front of a website’s address rests on the site’s certificate.

notes.front: What is mutual TLS (mTLS)?
notes.back: TLS in which both sides of a connection prove their identity, not just the server.
notes.explanation: It authenticates and encrypts the messages between two services, so that no unauthorised party can listen in or impersonate a legitimate request.
notes.example: Two parts of a banking application each proving who they are to the other before exchanging any data.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS)”

notes.front: What is a firewall?
notes.back: A device or program that controls which network traffic may pass between networks or hosts, following a security policy.
notes.explanation: It usually sits where a private network meets a public one, such as the internet, and blocks unauthorised access.
notes.example: A rule that lets web traffic reach a server and blocks every other kind of traffic.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “firewall”, from NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, SP 800-12 Rev. 1 and SP 800-35

notes.front: What is CIDR notation?
notes.back: A notation for describing a block of IP addresses, written as its start address and a subnet mask.
notes.explanation: Network settings use it heavily; for example, each node in a cluster can be given its own range of IP addresses this way.
notes.example: 10.244.1.0/24: one short entry standing for a whole block of addresses, instead of listing every address in it.

notes.front: What is version control?
notes.back: A system that records changes to files over time, so that you can get back any earlier version.
notes.explanation: It also lets you compare changes over time and see who changed something, and when.
notes.example: Git, the version control system most software projects use to store code.
notes.source: Pro Git (Scott Chacon and Ben Straub), §1.1 “About Version Control”
notes.sourceLicence: C · CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is a workload, in computing?
notes.back: An application running on a system: the work the machines are there to do.
notes.explanation: A workload can have several parts: a web server and a database might run as separate parts of one workload.
notes.example: A web shop made of a web server and a database is one workload, even though it has two parts.

notes.front: What is a public cloud, in terms of data centres?
notes.back: Data centres that rent out their capacity to customers.
notes.explanation: Over recent years, organisations have moved from running their own data centres to renting capacity in the cloud.

notes.front: A cloud dedicated to a single organisation, for security and control, is a {{c1::private}} cloud.
notes.explanation: A public cloud, by contrast, is open for widespread use, which helps with cost and scaling.

notes.front: When may bare metal be the right choice over a virtual machine?
notes.back: When a workload needs extremely fast access to hardware resources.
notes.explanation: With no virtualisation layer, there is no extra delay between the operating system and the hardware, and the hardware can be tuned for the task.

notes.front: Which three problems of bare metal machines do virtual machines address?
notes.back: Provisioning time, hardware utilisation and resiliency.
notes.explanation: No new hardware is needed for a new VM, several VMs share one physical machine, and VMs can move when a machine goes offline.

notes.front: How does a hypervisor protect virtual machines from each other?
notes.back: It partitions the hardware and assigns each VM its own share, keeping them isolated so one VM’s issues do not affect the others.
notes.explanation: Each VM can then run whatever operating system it needs.

notes.front: How is IaaS typically paid for?
notes.back: Pay as you go: you rent resources when you need them.
notes.explanation: This lets organisations defer large up-front spending on hardware and scale their resources up or down.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)”

notes.front: In PaaS, what does the consumer control?
notes.back: Its deployed applications, and possibly settings for the environment that hosts them; not the network, servers, operating systems or storage.
notes.explanation: The provider manages the infrastructure underneath, taking that work off the developers.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Platform as a Service (PaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: In SaaS, what does the consumer manage?
notes.back: Nothing underneath: not the network, servers, operating systems, storage or application features; at most a few user-specific settings.
notes.explanation: The provider runs the application and everything beneath it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Software as a Service (SaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: Why do APIs limit what can be asked of them?
notes.back: The limits help keep communication between programs stable and working.
notes.explanation: Without such a shared framework, applications are hard to grow and to integrate with each other.

notes.front: What big problem of self-contained applications does a client-server architecture solve?
notes.back: Regular updates: logic on the server can be changed without every user installing a new version.
notes.explanation: A self-contained program, such as a desktop word processor, must be downloaded and installed again for each update.

notes.front: How do the nodes of a distributed system collaborate?
notes.back: By exchanging messages over the network.
notes.explanation: The nodes can be hardware devices or software processes, programmed to achieve a common goal.

notes.front: Why is a non-distributed system riskier than a distributed one?
notes.back: If its one machine fails, the whole system fails.
notes.explanation: A distributed system can be designed to keep working, and produce the same result, even when some machines go down.

notes.front: In cloud computing, what can a node be?
notes.back: A physical computer, a virtual machine (VM), or even a container (covered in the Containers topic).
notes.explanation: Either way, the node gives a distinct unit of CPU, memory and network to the group.

notes.front: How does a cluster relate to a distributed system?
notes.back: A cluster is a kind of distributed system whose nodes are more closely linked to one another.
notes.explanation: Both spread work across several connected computers; in a cluster, those computers work especially closely together.

notes.front: Besides encrypting data, what does TLS let a client do?
notes.back: Positively identify the server it is calling.
notes.explanation: Encryption keeps third parties from seeing the data; identifying the server reduces the risk of talking to a fraudulent site.

notes.front: What are two other names for a digital certificate?
notes.back: A public key certificate, or an SSL certificate.
notes.explanation: Whatever the name, it helps prove identity and encrypt communication over a network.

notes.front: What does mTLS add to standard TLS?
notes.back: Both sides of the connection are validated, instead of only one.
notes.explanation: Traffic is then secure and trusted in both directions between client and server.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS)”

notes.front: What three things does version control let you do?
notes.back: Go back to earlier versions of files, compare changes over time, and see who changed something and when.
notes.explanation: It also means that if you break or lose files, you can usually recover them.
notes.source: Pro Git (Scott Chacon and Ben Straub), §1.1 “About Version Control”
notes.sourceLicence: C · CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; facts in our own words

notes.front: A start-up needs extra servers for a launch next week and cannot wait months to buy and install hardware. What approach fits?
notes.back: Cloud computing: renting compute, storage and network capacity on demand.
notes.explanation: Traditionally, more capacity meant buying new facilities or upgrading old ones, which is slow and costly.

notes.front: A building holds hundreds of servers on high-speed internet lines, with generators and powerful air conditioning. What is it?
notes.back: A data centre.
notes.explanation: Data centres are built to keep service running through adverse events such as power cuts.

notes.front: A physical server must go offline for repair, but the virtual machines on it must keep running. What can be done?
notes.back: Move the virtual machines to another physical machine, with little or no downtime.
notes.explanation: Because a VM is not bound to one piece of hardware, it is more resilient than a physical machine.

notes.front: A team rents virtual machines by the hour from a cloud provider and installs its own software on them. Which service model is this?
notes.back: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service).
notes.explanation: The provider supplies the compute, storage and network; everything above that is the team’s job.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)”

notes.front: Developers push their own application code to a provider’s platform, which runs it; they never manage servers or operating systems. Which service model is this?
notes.back: PaaS (Platform as a Service).
notes.explanation: In PaaS you deploy your own applications and the provider manages the infrastructure beneath them.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Platform as a Service (PaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: A company’s staff use a web-based email service in their browsers; the provider runs everything, and staff change only their own settings. Which service model is this?
notes.back: SaaS (Software as a Service).
notes.explanation: They use the provider’s application and manage none of the infrastructure beneath it.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Software as a Service (SaaS)”, from NIST SP 800-145

notes.front: A team’s app stores its data in Azure SQL Database, which Microsoft runs and maintains. What kind of offering is it?
notes.back: A managed service.
notes.explanation: It is a software offering maintained by a third-party provider.

notes.front: A weather app gets forecasts from another company’s program by sending requests in a fixed, documented form. What is it using?
notes.back: An API.
notes.explanation: An API is a defined way for programs to interact; the fixed form of the requests is what keeps the exchange stable.

notes.front: An online game runs on two hundred connected servers, but players see a single game. What kind of system is this?
notes.back: A distributed system.
notes.explanation: Autonomous computers linked over a network appear to the users as one coherent system.

notes.front: Five servers together run a website. What is each server called, in general computing terms?
notes.back: A node.
notes.explanation: A node is one computer working with others on a common task; the five together form a cluster.

notes.front: A shop’s website must stay online even if one computer crashes or is unplugged. What should it run on?
notes.back: A cluster: several nodes working together, so there is no single point of failure.
notes.explanation: Software on one computer goes offline when that computer does.

notes.front: A developer writes code against a cloud storage interface and never learns which disks hold the data. What is the interface providing?
notes.back: An abstraction: it hides the specifics underneath.
notes.explanation: If the code works with the abstraction layer, it works with the system, whatever is under the hood.

notes.front: Running a set-up script a second time leaves the system exactly as it was after the first run. What property does the script have?
notes.back: Idempotence.
notes.explanation: An idempotent operation gives the same outcome however many times it runs.

notes.front: A login page sends passwords across the internet in a form others can read and change. What protocol protects them?
notes.back: TLS, which encrypts the data between client and server.
notes.explanation: Without TLS, sensitive data can be traced and modified by others during transmission.

notes.front: Two internal services must each prove their identity to the other before they exchange data. What should they use?
notes.back: Mutual TLS (mTLS).
notes.explanation: Standard TLS validates only one side; mTLS validates both and also encrypts the traffic.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS)”

notes.front: A device lets web traffic reach a company’s servers and blocks everything else, according to set rules. What is it?
notes.back: A firewall.
notes.explanation: A firewall controls the flow of traffic between networks according to a security policy.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “firewall”, from NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1

notes.front: After a bad change, a developer needs yesterday’s version of a configuration file. What practice makes that possible?
notes.back: Version control.
notes.explanation: It records changes to files over time, so that you can get back specific versions later.
notes.source: Pro Git (Scott Chacon and Ben Straub), §1.1 “About Version Control”
notes.sourceLicence: C · CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a bare metal machine and a virtual machine?
notes.back: Bare metal: one operating system directly on physical hardware. VM: a software-defined computer sharing hardware with other VMs.
notes.explanation: Bare metal can give the best performance; VMs make better use of hardware and can move between machines.
notes.contrast: Dedicated hardware for one operating system, versus many software-defined computers on shared hardware.

notes.front: How do IaaS, PaaS and SaaS differ in what the provider gives you?
notes.back: IaaS: processing, storage and networks for your own software. PaaS: a platform to deploy and run your apps. SaaS: the provider’s finished applications.
notes.explanation: In summary: from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the consumer manages less and the provider more.
notes.contrast: Raw infrastructure, versus a platform for your code, versus finished software.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, “The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing”, §2 “Service Models”

notes.front: What is the difference between a node and a cluster?
notes.back: A node is one computer; a cluster is a group of nodes working together towards a common goal.
notes.explanation: Adding nodes to a cluster adds CPU, memory and network capacity.
notes.contrast: One machine, versus the group of machines.

notes.front: What is the difference between TLS and mTLS?
notes.back: TLS lets the client identify the server; mTLS validates both sides of the connection.
notes.explanation: Both encrypt the traffic; mTLS is the standard TLS protocol with the extra check in the other direction.
notes.contrast: One side proves its identity, versus both sides.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS)”
